Research objective.value: Review discourse on quality in qualitative research, meta-summarize quality benchmarks, and discuss opportunities and risks of AI in qualitative research.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: literature review / meta-summary of current qualitative-quality discourse

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Unsystematic narrative review. The article reports no database list, search string, date bounds, eligibility criteria, screening flow, included-study count, appraisal, extraction process, or synthesis procedure.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: not applicable/not reported for the review synthesis

Domain.value: cross-disciplinary qualitative-research quality and AI governance

Public or restricted data.value: source literature with unreported access mix

Sensitive-data status.value: no primary sensitive data collected; the review discusses risks to qualitative participants and vulnerable groups

Model family.value: No model was executed; examples discussed include ChatGPT, Meta AI, DeepSeek, Jenni AI, NVivo AI, and Otter.ai.

Exact model/version.value: not applicable; no model versions reported or executed

Prompting strategy.value: no prompts executed; prompting is discussed conceptually

Human role.value: Authors narratively synthesize literature and emphasize researcher interpretation, reflexivity, source verification, participant collaboration, and human oversight.

Unit of analysis.value: published claims and qualitative-quality constructs; exact source unit is not reported

Generated outputs.value: narrative synthesis, tables of qualitative-research types and NVivo capabilities/limitations, an adapted TACT framework figure, and recommendations

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Conventional in-text citations and adapted tables/figure; no reproducible review audit trail, included-study list, or source-to-synthesis map.

Principal results.value: The review frames quality around credibility, dependability, confirmability, transferability, authenticity, reflexivity, contextual sensitivity, and rigor. It says AI may aid transcription, scale, summaries, and pattern detection but introduces false references, repetition, bias, privacy/consent/accountability, and integrity risks. Recommendations include triangulation, member checking, peer debriefing, decision/audit trails, participant collaboration, cultural humility, institutional AI policy/training, and transparent reporting; AI cannot replace human interpretation/authorship.

Efficiency or cost results.value: qualitative workload/time-saving claims only; no runtime, token, monetary cost, or human-time measurement

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Extensive conceptual treatment of privacy, permission, consent, bias, accountability, vulnerable groups, algorithmic transparency, exploitation prevention, cultural humility, and human oversight. No primary-study protocol was required; funding and conflicts are reported as none.

Reproducibility resources.value: Open-access full paper only; no review protocol, search record, included-study list, extraction table, data, code, prompts, or model versions.

Author-reported limitations.value: No limitations of the review method are acknowledged. The conclusion instead lists generic qualitative-research limitations and calls for future work on trustworthiness and transparent epistemological positioning.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concerns: completely absent review methods prevent completeness/reproducibility assessment; sweeping efficiency/objectivity/inclusion claims lack a traceable selection process; conventional QDAS/transcription tools are conflated with LLMs; terminology errors and internally inconsistent objectivity-versus-bias claims weaken precision; some reliability/triangulation language imposes positivist sameness across heterogeneous paradigms.

Relationship to prior papers.value: Cites Dai et al. (2023) for LLM-prompted thematic-analysis workload reduction; no direct replication or shared-data study.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Supports audit criteria for reflexivity, contextuality, decision trails, participant involvement, source verification, privacy, and human oversight, but supplies no empirical benchmark or algorithmic novelty.
